parts.label: Part 3
parts.article:
Section three.

You will hear a university lecturer talking to a female student called Katie and a male student called John about writing essays.

First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five on page five.

Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

Morning, Katie. Morning, John. I want to talk about essays today and what the requirements are for this university, what kinds of things we look for when we're grading them. Okay? So let's look at those two sample essays I gave you last week. I asked you to read them and to think about their strong and weak points. Do either of you have any general comments or questions about the first one? Katie?

Um, well, the writer's made it quite clear what his own views are about this subject, but I thought in academic essays you weren't supposed to do that. I thought you were meant to present all the different arguments and just appear to be neutral about which one you think is best.

Students do sometimes come down quite firmly on one particular side, and that's okay as long as they can show that they've given balanced consideration to all the issues. Do you see what I mean?

Mm-hmm.

John, you're looking a bit uncertain. Did you want to say something?

Well, what if you don't feel as sure about the debate as this student?

There's another type of conclusion that's valid when you're writing at this level. People don't have to come down strongly on a particular side. They can say in the essay that the process of researching a particular topic has identified the importance of a range of studies that support different viewpoints, and then they return to the title of the assignment. Yes? And I'd say that it's a good idea to use some of the actual words that are in the title. It shows the reader that you're still on track. Okay?

Mm-hmm, yes.

Yeah, yeah.

Tony, can I just ask you something about the bibliography?

Of course.

Um, this person's used italics when he refers to book titles in the reference section, but I thought we had to underline them.

Actually, he's done it in the way we set out in the university study guide. That is the appropriate convention for titles. You might think it's trivial, but presenting references appropriately is one of the requirements of a degree at this level, so I wouldn't be doing my job properly if I didn't stress that. And once people are used to it, they don't generally have a big problem with it. Um, yes, Katie?

You mentioned the university's study guide. I looked in there to see what it said about quotations. Um, the essay's got a lot of quite long ones, and I was a bit surprised by that. I thought we weren't supposed to do that.

But using a range of quotations is a way of showing that you have actually read quite widely, isn't it?

Well, not really. Unfortunately, some students just pick out extracts to quote without actually reading the whole thing. It's really a matter of using quotations appropriately. I've marked essays in the past where literally every fourth or fifth sentence has been a quote, and that definitely isn't acceptable. You have to read widely, but you should be assimilating what you've read and, in general, presenting the ideas in your own words.

So when exactly should we use quotes?

Particularly where there are definitions involved, as there are here.

Generally speaking, I'd say that you need to be aware of words within the essay title itself that are possibly contentious, terms that need defining. For instance, this one here has the word culture in it. Now, although you probably have a rough idea of what that term means, you might not be able to articulate it very well. So why not cite someone else's definition rather than dream one up yourself?

Okay, any other comments on this first essay? What about the way the writer discusses research findings?

Um, one thing that struck me was the approach of the student to some of the things he'd read. He says things like, "We aren't given enough evidence," or, "We don't know how he got his results." When you're reading about someone's research, it's secondhand. You often don't get told how many people were studied or exactly what kind of questionnaires were used or how exactly the results were analyzed. But I've always felt that it's just up to me to go to the primary sources and find out.

It is important that you feel free to say if there are reasons why you can't make a clear judgment about something. But you don't have to, not at this level. It's almost as if we just take things for granted. Okay?

Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty on page six.

Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.

Now, let's look at the second essay then. Um, first of all, this essay title is in the form of a question, isn't it? Did you think this student answered the question?

Mm, yes. Yes.

Good, because really that's the bottom line. The minimum criterion for an assignment is relevance. Yes?

Sometimes people don't seem to see the words on the page, but you have to be very focused. Secondly, what about the overall structure? Would you say that the essay is well-structured?

Mm, yes, I would. I mean, sometimes writers mix different subtopics up, so it's quite difficult to follow the logic of the essay, but here I think they're separated very clearly.

Mm-hmm. Do you agree, John?

Yes. I mean, it is very clear, but is it okay to use subheadings and bullet points like this? I mean, in things like reports, they can be very useful, I know, but is it all right to use them in academic essays?

Well, my general feeling is that it's best just to use paragraphs to signal changes of topic. The beginning of a paragraph should signal what you're going to say in general, and then as you get to the end of the paragraph, you should be signaling what you're going to move on to next.

One thing I thought was really good about this essay was the way the writer always gives examples to support statements. He never just assumes that explanations are enough.

Yes, I'm glad you brought that up. I was going to mention it myself. As you say, it's very helpful for the reader.

Another thing that helps the reader is the way he uses words and phrases to connect ideas.

You mean things like however and on the other hand?

Yes, and finally, in addition.

Yes. That really is one of the hallmarks of a good essay. The content is the most important thing, of course, but there's no doubt that language can make the content clearer or otherwise for the reader. Now, you may feel at this early stage that your writing skills are rusty, but reading is the key, I think. As you read more and more extensively, you'll find that your own use of academic language will improve, and it'll get much easier to form your own ideas...

That is the end of Section Three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.question: Katy thinks it might be inappropriate for academic essays to

analyses.content: 录音中Katy明确指出作者表明了自己的观点，但她认为写学术论文不该这么做（weren't supposed to do that），这直接对应选项B的“表达个人观点”。
你可能会听到“present all the different arguments”，很容易因此错选A或C，但这其实是Katy认为写论文“应该做”的事，而不是她认为“不恰当”的事。

Um, well, the writer's made it quite clear what his own views are about this subject, but I thought in academic essays you weren't supposed to do that. I thought you were meant to present all the different arguments and just appear to be neutral about which one you think is best.

questions.question: The tutor says that in one type of conclusion students should

analyses.content: 导师在介绍另一种结论写法时，明确建议要回归到作业标题（return to the title），并最好使用标题里的原词，这与C选项完全对应。
你可能听到“don't have to come down strongly on a particular side”（不需要有强烈观点）就想选A，但这只是在说“可以保持中立”，并没有要求“保留/隐瞒（withhold）”自己的观点，不要过度解读。

There's another type of conclusion that's valid when you're writing at this level. People don't have to come down strongly on a particular side. They can say in the essay that the process of researching a particular topic has identified the importance of a range of studies that support different viewpoints, and then they return to the title of the assignment. Yes? And I'd say that it's a good idea to use some of the actual words that are in the title.

questions.question: What advice does the tutor give about quotations?

analyses.content: 导师建议在遇到需要下定义（definitions involved/terms that need defining）的地方直接引用别人的话，这完美对应B选项的“定义难懂的概念”。
录音前面男同学曾猜测引用是为了证明自己读得广（对应A选项），但导师马上用“Well, not really”否定了他，千万别把学生被否定的错误猜测当成导师的建议。

So when exactly should we use quotes? Particularly where there are definitions involved, as there are here. Generally speaking, I'd say that you need to be aware of words within the essay title itself that are possibly contentious, terms that need defining. For instance, this one here has the word culture in it. Now, although you probably have a rough idea of what that term means, you might not be able to articulate it very well. So why not cite someone else's definition rather than dream one up yourself?

questions.question: John suggests that the writer of the first essay should have

analyses.content: John认为，当觉得论文给出的证据不足时，应该自己去查阅一手资料弄个明白（go to the primary sources and find out），这对应A选项的“做更深入的研究”。
你可能会捕捉到“results were analyzed”这个词组而错选B，但这只是John在举例说明论文里“缺乏哪些信息”，他真正的建议在最后一句的去查一手资料。

Um, one thing that struck me was the approach of the student to some of the things he'd read. He says things like, "We aren't given enough evidence," or, "We don't know how he got his results." When you're reading about someone's research, it's secondhand. You often don't get told how many people were studied or exactly what kind of questionnaires were used or how exactly the results were analyzed. But I've always felt that it's just up to me to go to the primary sources and find out.

•　The tutor thinks that paragraphs should be used to structure essays.

analyses.content: Katy夸奖这篇论文没有把不同的子话题（subtopics）混在一起，而是将它们区分得非常清楚（separated very clearly）。
填空时容易忽略代词指代，录音中“separated very clearly”前紧跟着代词they，指代的就是前半句出现的“subtopics”，注意千万不要漏掉复数“s”。

Would you say that the essay is well-structured? Mm, yes, I would. I mean, sometimes writers mix different subtopics up, so it's quite difficult to follow the logic of the essay, but here I think they're separated very clearly.
John提问时说，副标题和项目符号在“报告”（reports）这类材料里确实很有用，对应题目中的“比在学术论文里更合适”。
题目问的是这些排版更适合“什么情况”，虽然题干词 bullet points 出现得很早，但一定要往后稳住听到“in things like reports”再下笔，同样别忘了复数“s”。

Yes. I mean, it is very clear, but is it okay to use subheadings and bullet points like this? I mean, in things like reports, they can be very useful, I know, but is it all right to use them in academic essays?
John特别指出，作者总是给出“例子”（examples）来支持自己的陈述（support statements），这里的support完美替换了题目里的backs up。
你可能会听到紧接着的“explanations are enough”，但那句话的意思是“作者从不认为光靠解释就足够了”，所以真正的支撑材料是 examples 而不是 explanations。
One thing I thought was really good about this essay was the way the writer always gives examples to support statements. He never just assumes that explanations are enough.
Katy赞赏作者使用了恰当的词汇和短语来连接“想法”（connect ideas），题目中的link直接替换了录音中的connect。
填空题听到“words and phrases”时很容易着急填进去，但结合整体语义，词汇和短语是“连接的工具”，真正被连接的宾语是最后的 ideas。
Another thing that helps the reader is the way he uses words and phrases to connect ideas.
导师明确总结道，当你觉得写作技巧生疏时，“阅读”（reading）才是关键，后面的“广泛阅读会提升学术语言”也印证了这一点。
录音前面聊了很多关于language和content的内容，容易让你在走神时填错，但只要听到“but”这个转折词，就能抓住导师给出的真正核心建议是 reading。

Now, you may feel at this early stage that your writing skills are rusty, but reading is the key, I think. As you read more and more extensively, you'll find that your own use of academic language will improve, and it'll get much easier to form your own ideas...
